item.title: Three-Dimensional Ultrasound Localization Microscopy Using Hadamard-Encoded Multipulse and 4D Denoising on a 256-Channel System with a 1024-element Matrix Array: A Feasibility Study in Human Kidney Transplants
item.description: arXiv:2611.26751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Three-dimensional ultrasound localization microscopy (3D ULM) enables volumetric visualization of microvasculature beyond the acoustic diffraction limit, but its clinical translation remains limited by long acquisition times, low microbubble (MB) signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and insufficient MB contrast, particularly on ultrasound systems with a limited number of acquisition channels. In this study, we developed an in-human 3D ULM framework for a 256-channel research ultrasound system equipped with a 1024-element matrix array. The framework combines diverging-wave Hadamard-encoded multipulse (HEM) transmission to enhance MB SNR with denoising strategy combining MB enhancement and four-dimensional non-local means filtering to improve MB contrast. The framework was implemented on a research ultrasound platform and evaluated in phantom experiments and four in vivo human kidney transplants. In phantom experiments, HEM improved the MB contrast ratio around 2 dB, while the proposed denoising strategy enhanced in vivo MB contrast by up to around 9 dB. 3D ULM reconstruction achieved a spatial resolution of approximately 84 um, as estimated by Fourier shell correlation. The number of reconstructed microvascular voxels increased exponentially with acquisition duration, reaching approximately 74% of the estimated saturated vessel density using 3000 volumes (~12 s). The subject with the highest histopathological injury exhibited quantitatively reduced microvascular vessel density, flow velocities, and mean perfusion index. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework enables high-quality volumetric super-resolution imaging and quantitative characterization of renal microvasculature using a 256-channel ultrasound system, providing a practical step toward the clinical translation of in vivo 3D ULM.

item.title: Optical Scintillation Imaging for Dynamic Source Tracking Dosimetry During Prostate HDR Brachytherapy
item.description: arXiv:2611.27146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy is highly conformal, but its accuracy depends on catheter and source placement, and clinical workflows lack real-time in vivo dosimetry (IVD) that verifies delivery without disrupting the procedure. We characterize a scintillator-based optical dosimeter integrated into a transrectal probe that tracks source position, speed, dose rate, and time-resolved cumulative dose. A 67 mm x 5 mm line scintillator is imaged by a CMOS camera through a 30-degree endoscopic lens; geometric and flat-field corrections remove barrel distortion and vignetting. Absolute dose was calibrated with a TOPAS Monte Carlo model of the probe's air-cavity geometry. The system was validated in a water phantom with an Ir-192 source and needles at radial offsets of 7, 10, and 15 mm. Response varied by $\pm$2\% along the 67 mm scintillator and was linear over 5-21 cGy/s ($R^2 \geq 0.995$). The Monte Carlo model showed a 3.75\% dose-rate reduction relative to TG-43 water-equivalent conditions. In phantom, the system resolved a 3 mm needle displacement, confirmed by CT. Measured dose-rate profiles agreed with Monte Carlo in peak magnitude and spatial distribution, and integral dose agreed within 1\%. By mapping dose directly to the measurement plane of a standard ultrasound transducer, this system provides high-resolution, time-resolved verification of HDR delivery and a clinical tool for detecting delivery errors with minimal changes to existing treatment protocols.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Willy, Megan Clark, Petr Bruza, Shauna McVorran, David Gladstone

item.title: ReCoFlow-MRI: Few-Step Conditional Flow Matching for GNL-Induced Nonlinear MRI Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2611.27590v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective: Accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction is challenging in the presence of gradient nonlinearity (GNL). GNL-induced nonlinear spatial encoding causes geometric distortions that compromise image-guided radiotherapy. Diffusion models require extensive sampling and rarely account for GNL. Flow matching shortens sampling, but velocity matching does not directly minimize the reconstruction error. We propose ReCoFlow-MRI, a conditional flow-matching framework for few-step GNL-corrected reconstruction. Methods: The calibrated GNL displacement field is integrated into the nonlinear encoding model to construct a distortion-corrected zero-filled image, which conditions a velocity field learned along a linear path from Gaussian noise to fully sampled images. The pretrained network is fine-tuned with a pixel-supervised endpoint loss on its five-step reconstruction. Results: On simulated fastMRI brain data, five-step ReCoFlow-MRI achieved the highest PSNR and SSIM among compared methods, including 128-step diffusion sampling. On MRI-Linac phantom and volunteer data, it achieved effective reconstruction and reduced the maximal geometric error from 24.95 to 2.12 mm, with 98.39% of the 3718 fiducial markers below 1 mm. Conclusion: ReCoFlow-MRI jointly addresses undersampling artifacts and geometric distortions within a few-step generative reconstruction. Significance: It provides a potential solution for fast and geometrically accurate imaging in image-guided radiotherapy.
item.dc:creator: Qidi Luo, Hongli Chen, Jialiang Zhang, Yuting He, Yang Gao, Chunyi Liu, Yaohui Wang, Feng Liu, Shanshan Shan

item.title: Receptor Abundance Alone Underpredicts Red Blood Cell Adhesion in Gaucher Disease
item.description: arXiv:2611.27960v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Red blood cells (RBCs) in Gaucher disease (GD) adhere abnormally to vessel walls and carry more Lutheran/basal cell adhesion molecule (Lu/BCAM), a laminin receptor. Whether receptor abundance sets this adhesion is untested. We simulated RBCs carrying stochastic Lu/BCAM-laminin bonds, calibrated a population on control donors, and predicted GD adhesion from the 1.3-fold receptor rise. On laminin and endothelium the data exceed the prediction 1.6- to 1.7-fold. Matching them requires 2.4- and 4.6-fold more binding-competent receptors, compatible with the estimated 5.7-fold rise in phosphorylated receptors. Neither a stiffer membrane nor higher bond affinity removes the shortfall at high shear stress. In sickle cell disease, given active-receptor counts, the model predicts the fall in adhesion under hydroxyurea within 1.4-fold, while total receptors rise. Adhesion likely follows receptor state more than abundance. Stiffening instead retains cells at a splenic slit.
item.dc:creator: Zhaojie Chai, Pierre A. Buffet, Melanie Franco, George Em Karniadakis

item.title: Physics-Based Differentiable Beamforming for Deep Learning-Based Contrast Enhanced Ultrasound Super-Resolution Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2611.10197v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ultrasound is widely used for vascular imaging because it is non-invasive, real-time, and cost-effective. However, its spatial resolution remains limited by diffraction to an order of the acoustic wavelength. This limitation is particularly restrictive for imaging of the microvasculature and high-resolution vector-flow-imaging. In this work, we present a multi-channel physics-based deep learning approach to super-resolve monodisperse microbubbles directly from multi-channel radio-frequency (RF) data. We also present a novel image-based metric for model evaluation. The proposed pipeline combines a learnable deconvolution network with a differentiable beamforming layer, enabling a direct deconvolution of the microbubble (MB) signature prior to image formation. By operating on multi-channel RF data, the method aims to improve localization robustness in the presence of dense microbubble populations and deconvolve the lateral direction in a relatively low-frequency regime (1.7 MHz) where MBs exhibit nonlinear behavior. The model is trained and evaluated on simulated data using monodisperse lipid-coated MBs over a broad range of acoustic pressures and microbubble densities. The proposed method improves the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compared to the single-channel approach. It achieves sub-wavelength axial and lateral resolution while slightly improving robustness to dense microbubble populations outside the training domain. It also demonstrates generalizability across transmit configurations without requiring explicit training on each transmit configuration.
item.dc:creator: Anass Hameddine, Bram de Wilde, Michel Versluis, Jelmer M. Wolterink, Guillaume Lajoinie
